prompt: With `Item` abstract, which line in `Desk` did the compiler refuse?
hint: An abstract class may be a type; it may not be an object.

choices.text: `Item mystery = new Item("Untitled");`
choices.why: Right: `Item is abstract; cannot be instantiated`.

choices.text: `Item item = new Book("Effective Java");`
choices.why: A variable of the abstract type holding a concrete `Book` is allowed and useful.

choices.text: `System.out.println(item.describe());`, since `describe()` calls an abstract method
choices.why: On a `Book`, `loanDays()` has a body; the call printed `14 days` once the other line was gone.

prompt: `Magazine extends Item` and writes no `loanDays()`. Which two changes would each make it compile?

choices.text: Add `@Override`, or make `loanDays()` in `Item` `final`
choices.why: `@Override` needs a method to annotate, and an abstract method cannot be `final`.

choices.text: Give `Magazine` a constructor, or remove `super(title)`
choices.why: The constructor is fine; the missing body is the problem.

choices.text: Make `Magazine` `final`, or make `Item` concrete again with a `return 0`
choices.why: A `final` class still needs every body; the second would work and bring back the default nobody chose.

choices.text: Give it the missing body, or mark the subclass `abstract` as well
choices.why: Right: `is not abstract and does not override abstract method`.

prompt: `describe()` in `Item` calls `loanDays()`, which `Item` never wrote. Why is that safe?
hint: On which objects can `describe()` ever run?

choices.text: Because the JVM skips a call to a method with no body
choices.why: Nothing is skipped; `describe()` printed the book's 14 days.

choices.text: Because `loanDays()` returns 0 until a subclass writes it
choices.why: An abstract method has no default value; it has no body at all.

choices.text: Every object it runs on is of a concrete class, which has the body
choices.why: Right: `Item` cannot be instantiated, and every concrete subclass must write `loanDays()`.

prompt: A method declared with no body, ending in a semicolon, for every subclass to write, is declared with the keyword ___.
hint: The same word goes on the class.

prompt: In `Loanable`, which method holds the fee rule itself?
hint: The one subclasses may not replace.

choices.text: `lateFeeCents`
choices.why: Right: it is `final`, and it calls the two blanks.

choices.text: `dailyFeeCents`
choices.why: That is a blank each subclass fills with a number.

choices.text: `maximumFeeCents`
choices.why: That is the hook with a default of 2000.

choices.text: The constructor, which sets the fee when the item is created
choices.why: The constructor sets only the title; the fee is computed per call.

prompt: What fee, in cents, does a `Dvd` charge for 30 days late?
hint: 150 a day, but its own maximum caps it.

prompt: `Book` does not override `maximumFeeCents()`. What maximum applies to a book?

choices.text: None: a book's fee grows without limit
choices.why: `lateFeeCents` always applies `Math.min` with whatever maximum the object has.

choices.text: 3000 cents, the last maximum any subclass declared
choices.why: Each object uses its own class's method; `Dvd`'s 3000 applies to DVDs only.

choices.text: 2000 cents, inherited from `Loanable`
choices.why: Right: it never mattered here, because 30 days at 50 cents is 1500.

prompt: Match each method of `Loanable` to what a subclass may do with it.
right_distractors: Must call it from its constructor

prompt: Why is `lateFeeCents` declared `final`, when no subclass in the lesson wanted to change it?

choices.text: So the rule holds for every subclass, even one written later
choices.why: Right: without it, `Ebook` would have compiled and charged -1.

choices.text: Because the JVM runs `final` methods faster
choices.why: Speed is not the reason given; the rule is.

choices.text: Because a method that calls an abstract method must be `final`
choices.why: No such rule exists; `describe()` in section 02 called one and was not `final`.

choices.text: So that subclasses can read `title`, which is private
choices.why: `final` on a method has nothing to do with field access; `title()` gives access.

prompt: Why are `dailyFeeCents` and `maximumFeeCents` `protected` rather than `public`?
hint: Who is meant to use them?

choices.text: Abstract methods cannot be `public`
choices.why: They can; `loanDays()` in section 02 was `public abstract`.

choices.text: So that `Fees` can call them without an object
choices.why: `protected` does not make anything static, and `Fees` calls only `lateFeeCents`.

choices.text: They are for subclasses to fill, not for other classes to call
choices.why: Right: other code should ask for `lateFeeCents`, the rule.

prompt: How does `Fees` print 450 cents as `4.50` without a `double`?

choices.text: `cents / 100.0`, rounded
choices.why: That is a `double`, which the program avoids.

choices.text: `String.format("%.2f", cents)`
choices.why: `%.2f` needs a floating-point argument.

choices.text: `cents / 100`, a dot, and `cents % 100` padded to two digits
choices.why: Right: 4, then 50; `%02d` would print 5 cents as `05`.

prompt: `new Loanable(...)` is forbidden. Who calls `Loanable`'s constructor?

choices.text: Nobody: an abstract class's constructor exists for documentation
choices.why: It runs for every subclass object; that is how `title` gets its value.

choices.text: Every subclass constructor, through `super(title)`
choices.why: Right: and `protected` says so.

choices.text: The JVM, once per class, when `Loanable` is loaded
choices.why: That describes a static initialiser; a constructor runs once per object.

prompt: `Special` printed `Special$1 extends Loanable`. What was created?

choices.text: An object of an anonymous concrete subclass of `Loanable`
choices.why: Right: the braces supplied `dailyFeeCents()` and the class has no name in the source.

choices.text: An object of `Loanable` itself, allowed because the body was supplied
choices.why: No object's class is ever `Loanable`; `getClass()` said `Special$1`.

choices.text: A copy of `Book` with a different daily fee
choices.why: `Book` was not involved; the anonymous class extends `Loanable` directly.

prompt: The map charges 500 cents a day and inherits the default maximum. How many cents for 10 days late?
Book and DVD differ only in their daily fee, a number, and in nothing else. What does the section suggest?

choices.text: An abstract method `dailyFeeCents()` in an abstract superclass
choices.why: That earns its place when subclasses run different code; here they differ in data.

choices.text: An interface `Feeable` with a constant per class
choices.why: An interface would still need a class per kind; the value can simply be a field.

choices.text: One concrete class with the fee as a field set by its constructor
choices.why: Right: no hierarchy is needed when only a value changes.

prompt: Which of these can an abstract class have? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A private field
choices.why: Yes: `title`.

choices.text: A constructor
choices.why: Yes: `protected Loanable(java.lang.String)`.

choices.text: A `final` method with a body
choices.why: Yes: `lateFeeCents`.

choices.text: An object of its own class, made with `new`
choices.why: No: that is the one thing it cannot have.

prompt: `item.lateFeeCents(30)` runs on a `Dvd`. Put what happens in order.
hint: The rule first checks whether the item is late at all.

prompt: A colleague adds `public int lateFeeCents(int d) { return 0; }` to `Book` to waive fees on books. What happens?

choices.text: Compile error: `overridden method is final`
choices.why: Right: the way to waive books is `dailyFeeCents()` returning 0, a blank the rule offers.

choices.text: It works, and books are charged nothing
choices.why: That is what `final` exists to stop.

choices.text: It compiles, and `Loanable`'s version still runs because it is `final`
choices.why: A `final` method cannot be overridden at all; the compiler refuses the file.

prompt: You are writing a `Report` superclass: every report prints a header, a body that differs per report, and a footer, in that order. How do you lay it out?
hint: The lesson's late-fee rule has the same shape.

choices.text: Three public abstract methods, and each caller calls them in order
choices.why: Then every caller must remember the order, and one will get it wrong.

choices.text: A concrete `print()` that subclasses override whole
choices.why: Each subclass then rewrites the header and footer, and they drift.

choices.text: A `final print()` doing all three, with the body as a `protected abstract` method
choices.why: Right: the template method, with the order owned by the superclass.

prompt: A method with a default body that a subclass may replace, like `maximumFeeCents`, is called a ___.
hint: One short word in English, and a fishing word in Portuguese.
